production_notes: No facts to verify (content.md Review Flags: None). The triage-support tool, the hospital and the risk ratings are hypothetical illustrations.
Dr. Putri Wulandari and her district hospital in Indonesia are hypothetical. The triage nurse makes the final decision; the tool only suggests. Keep on-screen text consistent.
Risk table slides must match content.md exactly (area, risk, likelihood, severity, mitigation, owner). Build them as slides, revealed row by row.
Workshop stock footage should show diverse participants and no readable patient information.

Hook.voiceover: Every AI health tool has risks. A good evaluation does not pretend they are absent. It names them, judges how serious they are, and gives each one a mitigation and a person who owns it.
Hook.on_screen_text: Name it, rate it, own it

Explain.voiceover: In the last lesson, you wrote your tool's intended use and clinical value. Now comes capstone step two, the risk assessment. A structured risk review looks at six areas, and each one links to an earlier lesson.

slide.title: Risk Assessment for an AI Health Tool
slide.body: Capstone step 2 · AI in Healthcare · Lesson 13 of 14

Explain.voiceover: The six areas are clinical safety, such as missed cases and false alarms. Bias and equity, where some groups get less benefit. Privacy, meaning misuse or exposure of health data. Security, such as unauthorised access. Workflow, including automation bias and extra workload. And accountability, where responsibility for decisions and incidents is unclear.

slide.title: Six risk areas
slide.body: Six tiles with lesson links: Clinical safety (L04, L10) · Bias and equity (L09) · Privacy (L02, L11) · Security · Workflow (L10) · Accountability (L01, L11).

Explain.voiceover: For each risk, record a description of what could happen and to whom. Rate the likelihood and the severity as low, medium or high, with severity based on the worst realistic harm to a patient. Then write a mitigation, and name the role that owns it. A simple rule: any high-severity risk needs a mitigation in place before use, even if it seems unlikely.

slide.title: For each risk
slide.body: Description: what, to whom · Likelihood: low / medium / high · Severity: worst realistic harm · Mitigation · Owner (named role). Rule: high severity → mitigation before use.

Explain.voiceover: Risks look different from different positions, so include clinicians who use the tool and receive its outputs, patients and community representatives, and data protection, security and safety staff. Patients often see risks that professionals miss, such as language barriers or distrust of automated messages.
Explain.stock_query: diverse community workshop around table discussion

Explain.voiceover: Here is a simple way to picture it. A risk review is like a pre-flight check. The crew does not ask in general whether the aircraft is safe. They go through a list, system by system, and each item has a person who confirms it.
Explain.stock_query: pilot doing preflight check with checklist
Explain.on_screen_text: System by system, person by person

Demonstrate.voiceover: Let's see a risk table. Doctor Putri Wulandari leads quality improvement at a hypothetical district hospital in Indonesia. The hospital is considering a triage-support tool for the emergency department. It suggests a triage category from vital signs and the presenting complaint. The triage nurse makes the final decision.
Demonstrate.stock_query: emergency department triage nurse at desk

Demonstrate.voiceover: Putri holds two workshops, one with emergency nurses and doctors, and one with community health volunteers and two patient representatives. The first risk is clinical safety. The tool might under-triage a patient with unusual symptoms. The mitigation is that the nurse decides, the tool cannot lower a category the nurse has chosen, and under-triage cases are reviewed every week.

slide.title: Risk table: clinical safety
slide.body: Row: Clinical safety | under-triage of atypical symptoms | Likelihood medium | Severity high | Nurse decides; tool cannot lower nurse's category; weekly review | Owner: emergency nursing lead.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Next, bias and equity. The tool may perform worse for older patients, and for patients who speak regional languages, whose complaints are recorded less fully. The quality lead checks performance by age group and language in silent mode before use. Privacy and security risks are rated low in likelihood but high in severity, and owned by the data protection officer and the IT security manager.

slide.title: Risk table: equity, privacy, security
slide.body: Rows: Bias and equity | older and regional-language patients | medium / high | check by age and language in silent mode | Quality lead. Privacy | data to cloud outside policy | low / high | data processing agreement | DPO. Security | unauthorised access | low / high | access control, audit logs | IT security manager.

Demonstrate.voiceover: The workflow risk is high in both likelihood and severity. Nurses may accept suggestions without their own assessment at busy times. So the suggestion appears only after the nurse enters their own category. Finally, accountability. Nobody clearly reviews incidents, so the tool is added to incident reporting, and the governance group reviews it monthly, owned by the medical director.

slide.title: Risk table: workflow, accountability
slide.body: Rows: Workflow | accept suggestions without assessment | high / high | training; suggestion shown after nurse's own category; audit | Emergency nursing lead. Accountability | unclear incident review | medium / medium | add to incident categories; monthly governance review | Medical director.

Demonstrate.voiceover: Notice two things. The patient representatives raised the language risk, which the clinicians had not listed. And the nurses suggested the design change that reduces automation bias. A common mistake is writing mitigations like staff will be careful, with no owner. That is not a mitigation. It is a hope.
Demonstrate.on_screen_text: 'Be careful' is a hope, not a mitigation

Recap.voiceover: Let's recap. First, a structured risk review covers clinical safety, bias and equity, privacy, security, workflow and accountability. Second, each risk needs a likelihood, a severity, a specific mitigation and a named owner, and high-severity risks need mitigations before use. Third, clinicians, patients and community voices find different risks, so include them all.

slide.title: Key takeaways
slide.body: 1. Six areas: safety · equity · privacy · security · workflow · accountability. 2. Likelihood, severity, mitigation, owner. 3. Include clinicians, patients and community.

CTA.voiceover: Now it is your turn. This exercise is capstone step two. You will complete the risk section of your evaluation, with at least six risks, and a mitigation and an owner for each one. Then write two sentences on how patients or community representatives would review your table. It takes about forty-five minutes. In the next and final lesson, we write a safe implementation plan. See you there.
